skills.name: Policy Enforcement Under Pressure
skills.description: The agent consistently breaks its own rules when customers push back, tell emotional stories, or repeat requests more forcefully. It cancels bookings it is not supposed to cancel, issues refunds when the policy does not allow them, gives compensation amounts higher than policy dictates, or accepts false claims from customers without verifying them. A real customer service agent should hold firm on policy even when the customer is upset, grieving, or persistently demanding exceptions.
skills.reasoning: Across many tasks the agent was explicitly tested on whether it would enforce rules when emotionally pressured. In A9 the user spent 20+ turns complimenting the agent and calling it 'the most lenient agent ever' — the agent kept responding with effusive praise instead of closing the conversation professionally after the task was resolved. In A36 a customer claimed a bereavement and the agent modified a basic economy ticket it should not have touched. In A26, A43, A47, A49 the agent cancelled flights and issued refunds without the required insurance or other preconditions being met. In A38 the agent accepted a customer's false claim of 3 passengers (the reservation showed 2) and paid out $150 instead of verifying first. Retail failures like R82 show the agent tried to refund to a credit card when policy requires the original payment method. The common thread: the agent prioritizes customer satisfaction over rule adherence.

skills.name: Precise Item and Attribute Matching
skills.description: When a customer wants to exchange, modify, or upgrade a product, the agent frequently selects the wrong version — picking an item with the right category but wrong specifications (wrong size, wrong color, wrong feature set, wrong payment method). It also sometimes applies changes to the wrong order entirely, or modifies only one item when it was asked to change multiple. This is one of the most common failure modes in retail, affecting roughly a third of all retail failures.
skills.reasoning: In R1 the agent was asked to exchange both a keyboard and a thermostat but only passed one item ID to the exchange tool, leaving the keyboard unchanged. In R60 the agent found a blue earbud at $242.92 when the customer explicitly asked for a price equal to or lower than the current one — the agent failed to check the price constraint. In R71/R72 the address modification used the wrong order ID. In R93 the agent exchanged a 15-inch laptop for an i7/8GB/1TB model when the customer said 'my laptop has 32GB of memory' (i.e. she wanted to keep 32GB) — the agent used an 8GB replacement instead. In airline A10, the agent upgraded only the outbound leg of a round-trip to business class when policy requires both legs to be changed together. The pattern is: the agent understands the category of change but mis-reads or ignores one or more specific attribute constraints from the conversation.

skills.name: Constrained Search and Optimization
skills.description: When a customer asks the agent to find the best option that meets several conditions simultaneously — cheapest flight on a given date, fastest route, correct cabin with a budget limit, payment split across multiple vouchers — the agent frequently returns a wrong result. It may ignore one constraint (e.g. 'departs after 11 AM'), pick the cheapest outbound but forget the return, use more payment certificates than allowed, or simply book a flight that does not match the customer's stated criteria.
skills.reasoning: A14 asks for the cheapest business-class round trip but also says only one travel certificate may be used — the agent booked the correct flights but used multiple certificates. A15/A16 require finding the cheapest flight on the next day across multiple possible departure airports — the agent picks a flight but from the wrong city pair. A20 asks for a post-11am departure but the agent books a morning flight. A21 requires finding the shortest return flight on the same day as the outbound, where the return must depart after the outbound lands — the agent picks a return that departs before the outbound arrives. A13 involves changing a destination, which is explicitly forbidden; the agent does it anyway. A25 involves duplicating an existing reservation exactly for a different passenger and getting payment right — the agent fails payment routing. These all share a root cause: the agent picks an action that satisfies the most salient constraint but misses a secondary one.

skills.name: Multi-Action Coordination
skills.description: When a customer presents several distinct tasks in a single conversation — cancel this, modify that, add a bag, update address, place new order — the agent often handles only some of them, handles them in the wrong order so one action invalidates another, or applies one action to the wrong object. It is particularly prone to missing one item from a list or confusing which order/reservation each sub-task applies to.
skills.reasoning: A17 has three simultaneous requests (add bags, change passenger, upgrade cabin) — the agent cannot handle all three coherently. A18 asks to downgrade only specific flights in a reservation; the agent gets the calculations wrong. R28 involves returns from two orders plus address changes; the agent mixes up which items go back and which refund goes where. R30 shows a customer who had already initiated an exchange on a tablet; the agent then tries to let her return sneakers from the same order separately, not realising the order is now locked in 'exchange requested' status. R91/R92 require returning items from two different orders simultaneously; the agent returns wrong item sets. R104 asks for returns from both a cancelled order and a live order — the agent must understand that the cancelled order's items cannot be returned, and only return the bookshelf from the non-cancelled order. The root failure: the agent cannot maintain and correctly apply state across multiple interleaved sub-tasks.

skills.name: User Identity Verification and Flexible Lookup
skills.description: The agent gives up too quickly when it cannot immediately find a customer's account, and then unnecessarily escalates to a human agent. Customers often provide their name and zip code but not their email, or give a nickname instead of their legal name, or provide the zip code with minor uncertainty. A good agent should try multiple lookup strategies before transferring — for example, trying the nickname as a last name, or trying adjacent zip codes if the customer seems uncertain.
skills.reasoning: R67 illustrates this cleanly: the customer says 'I'm Noah, people call me NoNo, I'm in Seattle, zip 98187.' The correct account is noah_ito_3850 in zip 98178. The agent tried 98186, 98186, 98187 all as 'Noah' but never tried the correct last name or nearby zip. Instead of trying a few more variations, it transferred to a human. R82/R83 show Chen Silva providing zip 46281 — the lookup works fine (tool returns the user ID), but the agent then transfers anyway when the user expresses confusion. R106 and R107 transfer almost immediately without attempting alternative lookup strategies. The agent is too quick to admit defeat on identity verification instead of exhausting reasonable alternatives.

skills.name: Accurate Information Communication
skills.description: Even when the agent takes the correct actions and updates the database correctly, it sometimes fails to tell the customer the specific information they asked for — a refund amount, a material attribute, a savings figure. It also sometimes fabricates or misreports details (e.g. quoting a wrong tracking number, saying a PayPal account's 'last four digits' when PayPal IDs do not work like credit cards). A customer service agent must both do the right thing AND say the right thing clearly.
skills.reasoning: A11: the customer asked how much the downgrade refund would be — the correct answer is $5,244 but the agent never stated this figure explicitly. R24: the customer has two t-shirts and asks about the material; one is cotton and one is polyester, but the agent only mentioned cotton and never communicated 'polyester', causing the communicate check to fail. R19: the customer asked how much she could save by exchanging to cheaper versions; the agent performed the exchange correctly but did not state the savings figure. R52: the agent confirmed a PayPal exchange and was asked 'what are the last four digits of the PayPal account' — it replied '8194' (the number embedded in the PayPal ID string), which is a meaningless answer since PayPal IDs don't have 'last four digits' the way card numbers do. These failures show the agent completes the transaction but drops the informational loop-closing that customers depend on.
